tests.topic: In 1462 Franciscan friars in Perugia opened the first Monte di Pietà, a pawn bank that lent small sums to the poor against a pledge and asked a little interest to cover its costs. The passage follows the quarrel this caused inside the Church, where rival preachers called any interest usury, until a council approved the banks in 1515, and argues that charity had to borrow the methods of the moneylenders it wanted to replace.

In 1930 the Futurist poet Marinetti published a manifesto of cooking that demanded the abolition of pasta, accused of making Italians heavy, slow and pessimistic, and opened a restaurant in Turin serving dishes meant to be touched and smelled as much as eaten. The passage treats the provocation seriously: it was ridiculed at once and changed nobody's lunch, yet it was the first time anyone claimed that a national dish is a choice and not a destiny.

The country that foreigners imagine as the home of the large family has had one of the lowest birth rates in Europe for decades. The passage rejects the easy explanation that young Italians no longer care about family and argues the opposite: because a child is still expected to receive everything (a stable home, a parent's time, grandparents nearby), couples wait until the conditions are perfect, and often wait too long.

A professor who has returned to Italy after twenty years in a British university and an older colleague discuss why Italian students are still examined mostly by speaking, one at a time, in front of the teacher. She finds the oral exam arbitrary and impossible to check afterwards; he answers that it teaches people to think aloud and defend an idea, and that a written test only looks more objective. Each concedes one point to the other.

Every spring until the 1960s tens of thousands of women travelled to the rice fields of Vercelli and Novara to pull weeds for forty days with their legs in the water. The passage recalls how in 1906 they won an eight-hour day before most factory workers had it, and how their songs survive in choirs and films, and asks why a job that everyone was glad to see replaced by herbicides is now remembered with something close to nostalgia.

In Sardinia about one person in eight carries the gene of thalassemia, an inherited blood disease that once condemned children to a life of transfusions; the gene was common because carriers resisted malaria better. From the 1970s doctors offered tests and counselling to couples, and births of sick children fell by more than ninety percent. The passage presents the programme as a public health success and gives room to the uneasy question it leaves: where prevention ends and selection begins.

The motorway bridge designed by Riccardo Morandi in Genoa was opened in 1967 as a symbol of modern Italian engineering, with its steel cables sealed inside concrete, and it collapsed in August 2018 killing forty-three people. The passage argues that the weakness lay less in the design than in a habit: the concrete that protected the steel also hid it from inspection, and a country that loves inaugurations finds little glory in maintenance.

When Carlo Scarpa restored the medieval castle of Verona as a museum between the late 1950s and the 1970s, he refused to imitate the old walls: he left a visible gap between ancient stone and new concrete and steel, and set the equestrian statue of Cangrande on a bare platform in the open air. The passage explains his idea that an honest restoration shows its own date, and the objection that the architect ends up more visible than the monument.

Since 2020 a line of seventy-eight steel gates rises from the seabed at the three mouths of the Venetian lagoon when a high tide is forecast, and St Mark's Square stays dry. The passage weighs the relief against the cost: the work took almost twenty years and was marked by a corruption scandal, every closure stops the ships of the port, and a lagoon shut too often stops exchanging water with the sea, so that saving the city could slowly damage what surrounds it.

On 4 May 1949 the plane carrying the Torino football team, winner of five championships in a row and supplier of almost the whole national side, crashed into the hill of Superga, and no one survived. The passage reflects on why this team is remembered more warmly than any that came later: it stood for a country getting up after the war, and, having died unbeaten, it was never allowed to decline.

In 1819 the twenty-one-year-old Giacomo Leopardi wrote fifteen lines about sitting on a hill near his home in Recanati behind a hedge that hides the horizon. The passage develops the paradox at the centre of the poem: it is the obstacle, not the view, that sets the imagination moving towards endless spaces and silences, and the poet who called pleasure an illusion ends by finding it sweet to drown in that sea.

In the 1780s the Bologna anatomist Luigi Galvani saw the legs of dead frogs twitch when touched with metal and concluded that animals contain their own electricity; Alessandro Volta, in Pavia, replied that the current came from the contact of two different metals, and to prove it built the first battery in 1800. The passage shows that the man who seemed to lose was also right, since nerves do work by electricity, and uses the dispute to show how a quarrel can serve science better than agreement.

Elsa Schiaparelli, born in Rome into a family of scholars, conquered Paris in the 1930s with a dress printed with a lobster designed by Salvador Dalí, a hat shaped like a shoe and a violent pink she called 'shocking'. Her rival Coco Chanel dismissed her as an artist who made clothes. The passage takes the insult as the real question between them (should a dress serve the woman who wears it or astonish those who look at her?) and notes which of the two houses survived the war.

For two centuries the most admired and best-paid singers of Italian opera were men castrated as boys to keep a high voice with an adult's lungs; Farinelli was courted by kings. The passage dwells on the hypocrisy of the system: the operation was forbidden by law, so every family told a story of an accident, while churches that barred women from singing hired the results, until the practice died out and the last of these singers left a recording in the early 1900s.

In 1550 the painter Giorgio Vasari published the lives of the Italian artists from Cimabue to his own day, and with them the idea that art had died with ancient Rome, been reborn in Tuscany and reached perfection in Michelangelo. The passage shows how much we still see through his eyes and how partial they were: a man from Arezzo working for the Medici gave Florence the leading role and left Venice and the rest of Italy in the background.

Divorce became legal in Italy in 1970, and in May 1974 the voters were asked whether to cancel the law; because the question was about repeal, those who wanted to keep divorce had to vote 'no'. The passage tells how almost sixty percent did so, including many in regions that the organisers of the referendum had counted as safely traditional, and reads the result as the moment the country discovered it had changed more than its leaders believed.

In 1950 the Italian state took hundreds of thousands of hectares from the great estates of the south and the Maremma and divided them among landless farm workers, building roads and small white houses on each plot. The passage sets the promise against the outcome: the plots were often too small and too dry to feed a family, and within twenty years many of the new owners had left for the factories of the north, though the old order of the absentee landlord never came back.

A young woman about to buy her first flat complains to a family friend, a retired notary, about the fee she must pay for an hour of reading aloud. He explains that in Italy the notary is a public official who answers personally for the validity of the sale, which is why disputes over who owns a house are rare; she replies that a profession whose numbers are fixed by the state and whose members often are children of notaries looks more like a guild than a guarantee.

Bread soup made from stale loaves, offal that butchers once gave to their workers instead of wages, wild herbs gathered along the ditches: the dishes that Italians invented in order not to go hungry now appear on the menus of expensive restaurants. The passage asks what is lost in the move, since a recipe born from the rule of wasting nothing means something different when the stale bread has to be bought on purpose.

A couple expecting their first child discuss which surname to give her, now that the Constitutional Court has ruled that the father's name can no longer be imposed automatically and a child receives both unless the parents agree otherwise. She wants both names; he is not against it but raises practical doubts (which one comes first, what happens in the next generation), and gradually admits that his real difficulty is telling his own father.

In the spring of 1945 the people of a village near Reggio Emilia sold an abandoned German tank, some trucks and a few horses and used the money to build a nursery school with their own hands; a young teacher, Loris Malaguzzi, cycled out to see it and stayed. The passage describes the approach that grew from there, in which children are said to have 'a hundred languages' and the teacher listens before explaining, and wonders why a method studied all over the world remains an exception in Italy.

A substantial share of Italian work is done without a contract: the builder paid in cash, the waiter registered for four hours who works ten, the private lesson with no receipt. The passage explains why the hidden economy is so hard to remove, since in poor areas it acts as a cushion that keeps families afloat, and why it remains a trap: no pension, no protection in case of accident, and unfair competition for every firm that follows the rules.

In 1898 the Roman zoologist Giovanni Battista Grassi proved that human malaria is carried by one kind of mosquito, Anopheles, and by no other; four years later the Nobel Prize went to the Englishman Ronald Ross alone, who had shown the mechanism in birds, and Grassi never forgave it. The passage links the dispute to its practical sequel: half a century later malaria disappeared from Sardinia after a vast campaign with DDT that failed in its declared aim of wiping out the mosquito.

In 1857 the Kingdom of Sardinia began to bore a railway tunnel more than twelve kilometres long under the Alps, a work that experts expected to take forty years with hammers and gunpowder. The passage tells how a drill driven by compressed air, invented during the works, cut the time to fourteen, and adds the irony of history: the tunnel was begun to join two provinces of one kingdom and was opened in 1871 as a frontier crossing, because Savoy had meanwhile been ceded to France.

After the earthquake of 1968 destroyed Gibellina, in western Sicily, the town was rebuilt some kilometres away as a modern city filled with works by famous artists, and Alberto Burri covered the ruins of the old one with a vast sheet of white concrete, cut by walkways that follow the former streets. The passage asks whether the work preserves the memory of the town or buries it for good, and reports that the inhabitants, living among sculptures and oversized squares, are themselves divided.

Italy covers roughly two square metres of soil with asphalt or concrete every second, although its population has stopped growing and millions of homes stand empty. The passage explains the contradiction (building on a field is cheaper than repairing an old house, and town budgets have long depended on building fees) and why it matters: sealed ground no longer absorbs rain or grows food, and soil lost in a year takes centuries to form again.

In 1978 Reinhold Messner, a mountaineer from the German-speaking valleys of South Tyrol, reached the top of Everest without bottled oxygen, which doctors had declared impossible, and two years later he repeated the climb alone. The passage presents his principle that a mountain should be climbed 'by fair means' or not at all, and the criticism it met: that an ethic of renunciation preached by a celebrated champion turned into another kind of record, and encouraged imitators less able than he was.

In December 1513 Niccolò Machiavelli, dismissed from office, tortured and confined to his small farm outside Florence, wrote to a friend that he spent the day quarrelling over cards at the inn and in the evening put on his court robes to converse with the ancient writers, and that from these talks he had composed a short book on principalities. The passage uses the letter to set the man, ironic and eager to be employed again, beside the adjective 'machiavellian' that has replaced him.

In 1877 the Milan astronomer Giovanni Schiaparelli drew a network of dark lines on Mars and called them 'canali', a word that in Italian may mean natural channels; in English it became 'canals', which are dug by someone. The passage follows the consequences, from an American observatory built to study Martian engineering to a whole literature of invasions, until a space probe photographed a desert in 1965, and concludes that the eye sees what the mind is ready to find, in lenses as in translations.

From the thirteenth century Italian cities passed law after law to limit what citizens could wear: the number of pearls, the length of a train, the width of sleeves, with fines and officials who stopped women in the street. The passage argues that the laws aimed less at morality than at keeping ranks visible and capital out of wardrobes, and that the very frequency with which they were rewritten proves they failed, since tailors invented a new fashion for every prohibition.

Leaving the opera house after a 'Rigoletto' set among gangsters in a modern city, an elderly season-ticket holder and her nephew, a drama student, disagree about what they have seen. She says the director has used Verdi to talk about himself and that the words sung no longer matched the stage; he answers that the costumes of the first night were modern dress for that audience too, and that an opera nobody dares to touch becomes a museum piece. They agree only about the tenor.

Around 1303 the Paduan banker Enrico Scrovegni, whose father Dante placed in hell among the usurers, had a chapel built and called Giotto to cover its walls with frescoes; in the Last Judgment the patron himself kneels on the side of the saved, offering a model of the building. The passage asks whether we should read the chapel as repentance or as an investment in reputation, and observes that a doubtful motive paid for figures that weep and embrace as no painted figures had before.

In the years after 1861 the new Italian state fought a long war in the southern countryside against armed bands that it called brigands, sending more than a hundred thousand soldiers and passing a special law that allowed military courts. The passage compares the two readings that still divide historians and families: common criminals paid by the exiled king, or peasants who had hoped for land from unification and received taxes and conscription instead; it suggests that many were both.

In the 1930s the Pontine Marshes south of Rome, which emperors and popes had failed to drain, were turned in a few years into farmland with canals, pumping stations and new towns, and thousands of families from Veneto and Friuli were brought to farm it. The passage separates the engineering, which ended malaria there, from the propaganda that the regime built on it, and adds a loss that nobody counted then: one of the last great wetland forests of the peninsula, of which a fragment survives as a national park.

In 1945 Enrico Mattei was appointed to close down the small state oil company; he disobeyed, found gas in the Po valley and built a national energy group. The passage recounts how he challenged the great foreign companies he nicknamed the 'seven sisters' by offering producing countries three quarters of the profit instead of half, and how his death in a plane crash in 1962, never fully explained, left open the question of whether he was a far-sighted public servant or a man who answered to no one.

At a farmers' market a customer proud of buying only local food talks with a stallholder who is an agronomy graduate. To her surprise he says that distance is a small part of a food's impact: tomatoes grown nearby in a heated greenhouse in winter can weigh more on the climate than those shipped from the south, and what matters most is the season and the way of farming. She objects that buying nearby also keeps farms and landscape alive, and he agrees that this is the better argument.

In 1965 Franca Viola, seventeen, from a Sicilian farming town, was kidnapped by a rejected suitor who counted on the custom, recognised by the penal code, that marriage cancelled the crime and saved the girl's honour. With her father's support she refused the wedding and took the man to court, where he was sentenced. The passage stresses how slowly the law followed the gesture: the article was abolished only in 1981, long after public opinion had sided with her.

The school reform designed by the philosopher Giovanni Gentile in 1923 put Latin, Greek and philosophy at the top and reserved to the classical high school access to every university faculty, a privilege that lasted until 1969. The passage argues that the hierarchy outlived the rules: in Italy an educated person may still admit without shame to understanding nothing of mathematics, and it asks what this habit costs a country that lives by manufacturing.

The owner of a small engineering firm near Brescia tells a careers adviser from the local high school that she has been looking for two welders for a year, while the papers speak of youth unemployment. The adviser replies that families see manual work as a defeat and that firms offer short contracts and low starting pay and then are surprised when nobody comes. Both end up asking whether the fault lies in schools, in wages or in the prestige attached to a degree.

For centuries a professor of medicine read the ancient author Galen aloud from a high chair while a barber cut the body below, and if the body disagreed with the book, the body was held to be wrong. The passage tells how at Padua Andreas Vesalius began to dissect with his own hands and published in 1543 an atlas of what he saw, and how in 1595 the university built a permanent wooden theatre in steep rings so that students could look down for themselves, and presents this as a change in what counts as proof.

In the 1970s Italian engineers built a train whose carriages lean into bends like a motorcyclist, so that it could run about a third faster on old winding lines without laying new track; they called it the Pendolino. The passage notes the paradox that followed: the idea was sold to half of Europe, while Italy itself chose in the end to build new, straight high-speed lines, and it compares the two answers to the same problem, adapting the vehicle or rebuilding the road.

Gian Lorenzo Bernini, brilliant, sociable and favoured by popes, and Francesco Borromini, solitary and difficult, a stonecutter's son who ended by taking his own life, competed for the commissions of seventeenth-century Rome. The passage contrasts Bernini's theatrical grandeur with the small church at the Four Fountains where Borromini made walls curve in and out, and corrects a favourite legend: the statue on Bernini's fountain in Piazza Navona cannot be shielding its eyes from his rival's church, which was built afterwards.

In a village in the Apennines at about a thousand metres, the mayor and the owner of the largest hotel discuss a plan to spend public money on new snow cannons and a ski lift. The hotelier says that without skiing the valley will empty within ten years; the mayor answers that at their altitude winters are now too warm even for artificial snow, which needs cold nights and a great deal of water, and proposes investing in walkers and cyclists all year round. Neither has a certainty to offer.

In 1924, short of famous riders, the organisers of the Giro d'Italia accepted the entry of Alfonsina Strada, the only woman ever to ride the men's race. The passage follows her over mud roads on stages of three hundred kilometres: when she arrived outside the time limit after a fall, she was allowed to go on unofficially because the crowds wanted her, and she reached Milan when two thirds of the men had given up; the following year her entry was refused.

Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa, a Sicilian prince who had published nothing, sent his only novel to two great publishers and was refused by both; he died in 1957 without knowing that it would appear the following year and become one of the most widely read Italian books of the century. The passage examines why critics of the time judged a story of aristocratic decline to be old-fashioned and reactionary, and how its famous sentence, that everything must change so that everything can stay as it is, is quoted as wisdom when the novel treats it as a bitter calculation.

In 1633 Galileo, nearly seventy, knelt before the Inquisition and denied that the Earth moves; the phrase 'and yet it moves' attributed to him appears in no document of the time and was first printed more than a century later. The passage argues that his true reply was a different one: confined to his house near Florence and going blind, he wrote his most important work on motion and had it printed in Holland, and the Church acknowledged its error only in 1992.

In a university seminar on communication a lecturer shows the posters that the photographer Oliviero Toscani made for a knitwear company in the 1980s and 1990s: a priest kissing a nun, a newborn baby still attached to the cord, a man dying of AIDS surrounded by his family, and never a sweater. One student calls it the courage to make people look at what they avoid; another says that suffering was used to sell jumpers. The lecturer asks whether both statements can be true.

At the end of the sixteenth century a circle of Florentine scholars and musicians, convinced that the ancient Greeks had sung their tragedies from beginning to end, tried to bring that lost art back by setting a whole story to a single voice that followed the rhythm of speech. The passage explains that their historical premise was largely mistaken and that the mistake was fruitful: instead of restoring Greek theatre they created opera, which Monteverdi's 'Orfeo' turned into great music within a few years.

In 1909 the Futurist manifesto declared that a roaring racing car was more beautiful than the Victory of Samothrace and called for museums and libraries to be destroyed as cemeteries of the past. The passage follows the contradiction through to the end: the painters who wanted to paint speed itself produced some of the most original Italian art of the century, their praise of war as 'hygiene' was answered by the death of their best talents at the front, and their canvases now hang, carefully restored, in the museums they wished to burn.

In 1516 the Venetian Republic ordered the Jews of the city to live on a small island in the district of Cannaregio where a foundry had stood, called the 'geto', and the name passed into every language. The passage shows the two faces of the decision: gates locked at night with guards the residents had to pay for and houses forced to grow upwards for lack of space, but also the right to stay, to trade and to pray in a century when other states simply expelled them.

For six centuries much of central Italy was farmed under a contract by which a peasant family lived on a landowner's farm and gave him half of everything it produced. The passage shows how this arrangement, abolished by law between 1964 and 1982 as unjust, drew the landscape that visitors to Tuscany admire (the isolated farmhouse on the hill, rows of vines between strips of wheat and olive trees), and notes the irony that the houses the sharecroppers were glad to leave are now sold as luxury villas.

In 1815, after Napoleon's fall, the sculptor Antonio Canova was sent to Paris to reclaim the paintings and statues that French armies had carried off from Italian cities under the terms of imposed treaties. The passage recounts his partial success (about half came back, and a huge Veronese was judged too fragile to travel and stayed in the Louvre) and an unexpected effect: many recovered works did not return to their churches but entered public museums, as if the theft had taught the robbed how to show them.

In the spring of 1986 more than twenty people died in northern Italy after drinking cheap wine to which a producer had added methanol to raise its alcohol content, and within weeks exports collapsed. The passage argues that the worst scandal in the history of Italian wine was also its turning point: controls were tightened, and a sector that had sold quantity at low prices understood that it could survive only by producing less and better.

In 1958 Sofia Corradi came back to Rome with a master's degree from an American university and was told at the office window that her year abroad counted for nothing; she spent the next three decades persuading rectors and ministers that study in another country should be recognised, until the Erasmus exchange was born in 1987. The passage credits the programme with making a generation feel at home in Europe and gives weight to the objection that its grants are too small for those whose families cannot add the rest.

Two old friends, an architect and a retired history teacher, stop in front of the glass and white stone building that an American architect designed to house the Ara Pacis, the altar of Augustus, opened in 2006 as the first important modern work in the centre of Rome for many decades. The teacher finds it a foreign body among baroque churches; the architect reminds him that every one of those churches was once the modern building that offended somebody, and that a city which only preserves has decided to stop having a history.

By the early nineteenth century fewer than a hundred Alpine ibex were left in the world, all on the slopes of the Gran Paradiso, and in 1856 King Victor Emmanuel II made the massif his private hunting reserve, with guards against poachers and paths for his horse. The passage draws out the paradox that the animal was saved by a man who wanted to shoot it himself, and that the reserve, given to the state, became in 1922 Italy's first national park, from which every ibex now living in the Alps descends.

In the 1930s, while the regime preached national self-sufficiency in culture too, the young writers Cesare Pavese and Elio Vittorini translated Melville, Faulkner and Steinbeck, and in 1941 Vittorini assembled a great anthology of American writing that the censor allowed to appear only without his commentary. The passage argues that the America of these translators, most of whom had never crossed the ocean, was partly an invention: a country imagined as young and free in order to say what could not be said about their own.

Just after the war, with the studios in ruins, Italian directors took their cameras into the street and gave the leading parts to people who had never acted: the father in 'Bicycle Thieves' was a factory worker. The passage sets the admiration these films won abroad against the irritation they caused at home, where a government minister complained that dirty linen should be washed in the family, and against the fate of the worker himself, who found no steady work again in either the factory or the cinema.

For centuries the popes based their claim to rule central Italy on a document in which the emperor Constantine was said to have given them the western half of the empire. In 1440 the humanist Lorenzo Valla proved it a forgery with a new kind of evidence: its Latin contained words and titles that did not exist in Constantine's time. The passage observes that he wrote in the service of a king at war with the pope and nevertheless ended his career as a papal secretary, and asks whether an interested motive weakens a sound proof.

On a terrace above the steep vineyards between Conegliano and Valdobbiadene, recognised as a World Heritage landscape, a winegrower and a primary school teacher who lives beside his rows talk about the success of the sparkling wine sold all over the world. She speaks of vines planted where woods and meadows used to be and of spraying a few metres from the school garden; he answers that the wine has stopped young people leaving and that the hillside vines, worked by hand, should not be blamed for the new plantations on the plain. They look for a rule both could accept.
